'''Marianne Elizabeth Bronner''' (born December 1952)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marianne Bronner |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/marianne-bronner-maapv6/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |language=en-US}}</ref> is a Hungarian-American developmental [[biologist]] who currently serves as [[Edward B. Lewis]] Professor of Biology<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Marianne Bronner Awarded Vilcek Prize in Biomedical Science – Pasadena Now|url=https://pasadenanow.com/main/marianne-bronner-awarded-vilcek-prize-in-biomedical-science|website=pasadenanow.com|access-date=2025-11-28|date=February 4, 2025|last=Dajose|first=Lori|ref=pasadena vilcek}}</ref> and an executive officer for [[Neurobiology]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]]. Her most notable work includes her research on the [[neural crest]].<ref name="crb">Bronner, Marianne E. "A career at the interface of cell and developmental biology: a view from the crest." Molecular biology of the cell 23.21 (2012): 4151-4153.</ref> focusing on the study of cellular events behind the [[Cell migration|migration]], [[Cell Differentiation|differentiation]], and formation of neural crest cells.<ref name="bronlab">{{Cite web |title=Marianne Bronner {{!}} Biology and Biological Engineering |url=https://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/marianne-bronner#publications-b4dab8c0-tab |access-date=2023-04-08 |website=www.bbe.caltech.edu}}</ref> She currently directs her own laboratory at the [[California Institute of Technology]] called the Bronner Laboratory, and she has authored over 400 articles in her field.<ref name="bronlab" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Library Feeds |url=https://feeds.library.caltech.edu/people/Bronner-M-E/ |access-date=2023-04-08 |website=feeds.library.caltech.edu}}</ref>

==Early years==

Bronner was born in [[Budapest, Hungary]] in 1952 to parents who were both survivors of the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Discovery's Crest: A Profile of Marianne Bronner|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/discoverys-crest--a-profile-of-marianne-bronner-65133|website=The Scientist|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en|first=Anna|last=Azvolinsky}}</ref><ref name="crb" /> When she was four, the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956]] prompted her family to flee Hungary into Austria, where they stayed for six months before immigrating to the United States.<ref name="crb" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Marianne Bronner: Advancing Stem Cell Research and Equity in Science|url=https://vilcek.org/news/marianne-bronner-advancing-stem-cell-research-and-equity-in-science/|website=Vilcek Foundation|access-date=2025-11-28|language=en-US|date=February 3, 2025|ref=vilcek}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

==Education and career==

Bronner attended [[Brown University]] for her undergraduate studies in 1971.<ref name=crb /><ref name=":1" /> After she graduated from Brown University in 1975, she decided to apply to the [[biophysics]] graduate school program at [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref name=crb /> Once there, she decided to take an undergraduate course in [[developmental biology]],<ref name=brc>Bronner-Fraser, M. "Investigator profile. An interview with Marianne Bronner-Fraser, Ph. D. Interview by Vicki Glaser." Zebrafish 2.2 (2004): 71-75.</ref> joining Alan Cohen's laboratory.  From there, she continued to specialise in the field,<ref name=crb /> completing her thesis in 1977 on neural crest cell developmental potential by injecting an individual quail neural crest cell (which Cohen had [[Cloning|cloned]]) into a chicken embryo and studying how the cell developed.<ref name=":1" />

Once Bronner graduated from Johns Hopkins University with her Ph.D. in 1979,<ref name=":0" /> she began teaching at the [[University of California, Irvine]].<ref name=crb />  Bronner spent 16 years at the university teaching and researching and eventually became the associate director of the Developmental Biology Center.<ref name=crb />

In 1988, Bronner and her husband, fellow biophysicist [[Scott E. Fraser]], did a study that showed neural crest cells being [[multipotent]] in an embryo for the first time. A similar study in 2015 via different methods showed similar results.<ref name=":1" />

She was promoted to a Professor at University of California, Irvine in 1990.

In 1996, Bronner left the University of California, Irvine and moved her laboratory to the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0" /> In 2001, Bronner became Chair of the Faculty at the California Institute of Technology, being the first woman to hold the position.<ref name="brc" /><ref name=":0" /> She held that position for two years<ref name="brc" /> before becoming the director of the [[Beckman Institute at Caltech|Beckman Institute]] at the California Institute of Technology in 2019.<ref name=":0" />

==The Bronner Laboratory==

Bronner has been directing a laboratory at the California Institute of Technology since she first arrived at the university.<ref name=brc /> The lab focuses most of its research on how neural crest cells arise, the factors involving their migration from the [[neural tube]] to different positions in the [[embryo]], and the evolution of these cells.<ref name=brc /><ref name=":1" /> One project focuses on characterizing the structures involved with neural crest cell movements.<ref name="ccc">"Lab Research." Bronner Lab. Web http://www.bronnerlab.com/lab-research.html</ref> Another project in the lab focuses on comparing the mechanisms behind neural crest invasive behavior and the mechanisms that allow for adult derivatives to become migratory and invasive.<ref name=ccc />

== Personal life ==
Bonner married [[Scott E. Fraser]], a fellow biophysicist, whom she worked with on several studies. She has two children, and was one of the few women in her fields to be a mother in addition to her work.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

==Awards and honors==
* [[Vilcek Prize in Biomedical Science]] (2025)<ref name=":2" />
* Elected member, [[National Academy of Sciences]] (2015)
* [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences|American Academy of Arts & Science]], Fellow (2009)
* Edwin G. Conklin Medal from the [[Society for Developmental Biology]] (2013)
* [[Women in Cell Biology]] Senior Leadership Award (2012)
* BUSAC Award for Excellence in Teaching (2001 & 2005)
* [[Javits Neuroscience Investigator Award]] from the [[National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke|National Institute Of Neurological Disorders And Stroke]] (2002–2009)
* ASCIT Award for Excellence in Teaching (1997 & 1998)
* Distinguished Research Award from the [[University of California, Irvine]] (1994)

==Professional societies==
* [[Beckman Institute at Caltech|Bekman Institute at California Institution of Technology]], director (2019–present)<ref name=":0" />
* International Society for Differentiation, president (2013–2014)
* International Society for Developmental Biology, secretary (2010–2013)
* [[Gordon Research Conferences]], board of directors (2006–2013), chair (2012)
* [[Society for Developmental Biology]], president (2009)
* Sontag Foundation, scientific advisory board member (2006–present)
* [[American Society for Cell Biology]], council member (1994–1997)
